title: Context strip
summary: Adds P16 Context strip (draft): when a machine's controls pick part of a bigger whole (a multisample synth's zones, a long wavetable, a built-in recording, or a sampler whose drawing is a close-up of part of its sample) and the drawing is a close-up, a small static locator of the whole sits under the header, or replaces the header as a piano or the sample's silhouette with no values (at most four controls). Any machine can use it; the conditions are defaults. Plus the matching craft.md and P8 exceptions.
rationale: Asked for by the guidelines' owner on 2026-11-04: engines can carry a top strip with grid context, such as where on a keyboard a multisample engine is, or where in a larger whole. On 2026-11-05 the owner asked that the strip can also replace the grey header entirely and show a piano with no titles or values, as the stock OP-XY multisampler page does, and shared a screenshot of that page as the reference: a plain grey bar over the whole range with only the playable span drawn as keys. The image is kept out of the repo; the pattern takes the approach, not the artwork. Grounded in open-xy staging 6b2d113: Input has note activity but no pitch; covering y 0-20 hides the stock header; five to eight controls use page_header.hpp; ux.md asks for real-unit header values, a convention catalog review checks, so the trade is stated. Later on 2026-11-05 the owner asked that the strip still work for samples in the right cases, so the sampler exclusion becomes a condition (only when the drawing is a close-up of part of the sample), built from the overview with the two-outline build an earlier audit found workable. Later the same day the owner said the strip can be for any engine, since it's a pattern, so its categories are all and its conditions are defaults that a screen can break with a reason. The sample form stays in place of the header until an under-header sample form is worked out. Precedents: toro-blocks and theseus-tower are unaffected; neither has a context strip, and nothing here changes a rule they rely on.

changes.content:
## P16 · Context strip

**The idea.** A draft pattern: no audited screen uses it yet; the three mocks in its proposal (`training/proposals/2026-11-04-context-strip/`: `mock-rest.png`, a multisample synth under the header; `mock-header.png`, the same in place of it; `mock-sample.png`, a sample engine) show the intent. Any machine can play from something bigger than one picture: a multisample synth's zones across the keyboard, a long wavetable, a recording built into the engine, the sample a sample engine plays, a sequencer's long pattern. When the controls pick part of that whole and the drawing is a close-up of the part, I put a small, static map of the whole at the top of the page, either under the header or in place of it (below): a ruler of the whole and an open bracket on the part the controls pick. Under the header, each half of the bracket uses the close-up's corner form, the same 7 px arms joined by a short upright, so the bracket and the frame read as the same mark; that's what ties the two together. In place of the header, the window of keys is the selection and the band is the header's own place, so the tie is the header itself. The bracket is shorter, heavier and brighter, because it's the part that moves; the drawing stays the picture every control changes, and the map only answers "which part of the whole is this?". It's the top-edge partner to P5's activity strip: that one says what's happening, this one says where you are.

**Why it works.** A close-up loses its frame of reference. With one zone's sample drawn large, the player can't tell which part of the keyboard it covers; with one frame of a long table drawn large, they can't tell how far through it they are. A locator is how drawings have always answered that, so it reads as part of the drawing rather than an interface. Under the header that means a ruler: no slider, no filled bar echoing the header, no text. In place of the header, the band is the header's own bar, so the map takes over the OP-XY's own furniture instead of adding a second piece.

**When it's there.** It's a pattern, not an engine feature, so any category can use it; what decides is the screen, not the category. Two things decide it. The first is a default: the controls select part of a whole that the drawing doesn't show (zones, a table, a recording, a sample). A screen can use the strip for some other kind of whole, saying why in a sentence. The second always holds: I can say in one sentence what the map tells the player that the drawing doesn't. A map of nothing the player needs is a panel, so without that sentence there's no strip. With both, it's part of the resting page, as `craft.md` allows.

- **Not P4.** When the whole is a short ordered set the drawing can stack (P4's five or six layers), the stack already shows where you are. P16 is for wholes a stack can't show: a span of the keyboard, a table too long to layer.
- **Not P13.** If a control's only picture is a keyboard (a scale, a kit's spacing), that's P13's corner keyboard.
- **A sampler, when its drawing is a close-up.** A sample engine's obvious subject is its sample overview (`categories.md`), and then a map of the sample would draw the same thing twice, so there's no strip. But when the drawing is a close-up of part of the sample (the stretch between the markers, a slice, a grain window, or a loop when the engine has its own loop controls), the whole sample is exactly the map it needs. For now that map goes in place of the header only (below). A synth that carries its own recording works the same way, except that its map is static artwork, since its recording never changes.

**Under the header or in place of it.** The map has two forms, and the machine picks one.

- **Under the header** keeps the stock header, titles and values as they are, and the map is a slim ruler below it. It's the default, and the only form for a machine with five to eight controls, whose header has to show which page the encoders edit. A sample map has no under-header form yet, so a sampler with five to eight controls goes without one until someone works it out.
- **In place of the header** gives the whole band, y 0–20, to the map, the way the stock multisampler page gives its header to the keyboard: the whole range as a plain grey bar, and only the part the controls pick drawn as real keys, with no titles or values. I take the approach from that page, not its artwork. The artwork covers the top 20 px, which hides the stock header (`display.md`, Artwork), and builds the band from static artwork and nodes; it uses no text slots. It's for a machine with at most four controls, where the map is what the player needs most and the drawing makes every control read on its own, since no number on screen will. The page trades the header's real-unit values (`ux.md`, Controls) for the map, so I say so in the handoff and the machine's README, because catalog review checks machines against that convention.

**Build it.**

- **Drawn in the screen's language.** The ruler, bracket and corner marks belong to the drawing's own language (`craft.md`, One drawing language): an atlas gets a locator inset, a section drawing gets a detail mark.
- **In place of the header.** The band is the whole range as plain `#4B4B4B` segments, one per octave with 1 px gaps, 19 px tall; eight octaves at 60 px each echo the stock header's eight 60 px steps. The part the controls pick (the playable span, an octave, a transpose window) is drawn as keys at the same scale in `#AFAFAF`, over a black backing the size of its segment: the white keys are one closed outline with the black keys notched in from the top and the key gaps (on whole pixels) from the bottom, which fits an octave in 48 points. The backing and the keys are two nodes with the same origin and transform, so they move as one part (`display.md`: parts that meet share an outline or a pivot) and the segments under them stay static. Moving the window costs two nodes; at rest, nothing. The window is the bracket in this form, so there's no other selection mark, and it has a fixed width; a selection whose width changes (zones of different sizes) uses the under-header form instead. The drawing's frame starts a little below the band.
- **Where and how big, under the header.** About 6 px under the header (below y 20 with the stock header, below y 38 with the two-page header, `tokens.json` → `header`) and about 10 px tall: my starting values, slimmer than P5's 16 px bottom strip (`body.stripTop`–`stripBottom`). It spans exactly the close-up's frame (the frame's corner marks sit at the map's two ends), not the header's columns, and the gap lets the drawing own it; together those keep it from reading as a second header row.
- **A sample as the map, in place of the header.** The whole sample comes from the overview's 96 bins (`display.md`, Sample overview), which change with every sample, so it can't be static artwork. A static black backing covers y 0–20 first, so the stock header never shows around the silhouette or while the band is empty (`display.md`, Artwork). Over it go two mutable outlines, filled `#4B4B4B` with no stroke (a stroke would double at scale 2). Each is at scale 2 and authored within ±60.25 px, so it spans 241 px drawn, and the two overlap 2 px at the middle. The overlap is meant to hide the seam: separately placed outlines can land apart on the device (`display.md`, Artwork), so whether it does is pending a device check. The silhouette, the close-up and the markers share one mapping: bin *i* covers x 5*i* to 5*i* + 5 across the band, and a marker at fraction *f* of the sample sits at x 480*f*. Each half has 16 points spread evenly over its 241 px along the top, and 16 back along the bottom. A point takes the highest high (top) or lowest low (bottom) of the bins whose centres lie within half a point-spacing of its x, each at least ±0.5 px authored (1 px drawn) so quiet stretches still enclose area, starting mid-way along the top so the closing edge is long. Every mutable outline in a frame has the same point count (`draw.hpp`, `Path<Points>`), so these 32 set the drawing's count too. They re-key only when the overview's `generation` differs from the one the machine stored. `display_reset` clears the stored one, so the first frame after a reset, which has to set every element anyway (`display.md`, Frame), redraws as well. That's two outlines on the frame a sample arrives and none at rest; the close-up and markers add to it (below). While `assigned` or `loaded` is 0 the band shows only the backing, and the line saying how to load a sample goes in the drawing's area.
- **The sample's markers bound whatever the close-up shows.** They're two 5 px squares in `#969696` on the band's bottom edge. They're small marks rather than lines, so they read as points on the band rather than a cursor, and dimmer than the close-up, so the drawing stays brightest. They follow the overview's `begin` and `end` when the close-up is the stretch between stock's markers (stock or `stockShift` owns them, SDK 1.10; they follow edits in any frame). When the close-up is the engine's own slice, grain window or loop, they follow its own controls through `Input`.
- **The sample's close-up.** The drawing gets the other two outlines, at the same 32 points, and draws the stretch between the markers the same way the band draws the whole: two halves filled `#AFAFAF` with no stroke, each at scale 2 and 193 px drawn (authored within ±48.25), overlapping 2 px (the same seam caveat). It uses the same mapping, stretched: x 48 to 432 runs from `begin` to `end`, and each half has 16 points spread evenly over its 193 px. When the stretch has at least 32 bins (so each half's 16 points are at least a bin apart), each point takes the highest high and lowest low of the bin centres within half a point-spacing, so a long stretch keeps its peaks. Below 32 bins, as most close-ups are, every point takes the straight line between the two nearest bin centres. Every point then lies on a line between real values, so nothing is invented and there are no plateaus, though a peak or trough at a bin centre that falls between two points can be shaved by a pixel or two at this scale. It's never less than one bin. Joining real values with straight lines invents nothing between them, so the close-up shows what the device knows (`display.md`, Sample overview) without promising detail it doesn't have, and the band and the close-up share one mark. The other way is a figure driven by the engine's own controls (a grain's envelope, a slice's shape) instead of the audio. `mock-sample.png` shows the first.
- **What the sample form costs.** The band re-keys on `generation` alone. The close-up re-keys then too, and whenever `begin` or `end` (or the engine's own bounds through `Input`) moves, because they follow edits in any frame without `generation` changing. A new sample costs all four outlines and both markers on one frame; every edit of `begin` or `end` moves a marker node and reshapes the two close-up outlines. Either way it's a filled outline reshaping, a moving fill (`constraints.md`, Moving fills), so that's pending a device check too. At rest it costs nothing.
- **The ruler is static artwork and a guide.** The whole is the engine's own fixed data (its zone map, its table, its recording), so the ruler is authored once and never redraws. Its marks are uniform and sparse, on whole pixels, hairline (1 px) in `#646464`: a keyboard gets a tick per C, a table a tick every nth frame so ticks stay at least 3 px apart, with n chosen for the table's length. A strip w px wide gives w/keys px a key and 12 × that between C ticks (480 px over all 128 notes is 3.75 and 45; the mock's 384 px over six octaves is 5.33 and 64). Zones are told apart by position: the baseline is 2 px in `#646464`, broken by a 3 px gap at each split, not by shade.
- **The bracket is two nodes.** A left and a right piece in `#AFAFAF`, 1.5 px, about 6 px tall, each one closed outline (8 points): two corners with 7 px horizontal arms joined by an upright. It sits above the baseline, at least 1 px clear of it, with each upright centred over its split gap, so the splits it points at stay open; the same offset on both sides. It's open in the middle, so its width follows the selection by moving the pieces, never by scaling. Driven by the controls through `Input` like every other part, easing 0.15–0.2 s. Each edit costs two nodes; at rest it costs nothing. The brightest thing on screen stays in the drawing.
- **The close-up's frame.** Four corner marks: under the header, at the map's ends and the drawing's top and bottom; in place of the header, simply around the drawing. Each is one closed outline with 7 px legs both ways, hairline (1 px) in `#646464`. The same corner form and arm as the bracket; taller, lighter and quieter on purpose.

**Pitfalls.**

- **Possible isn't the bar.** open-xy says what the device can draw; the OP-XY's own look decides what belongs on the page. A map that's buildable but busy, bright or labelled fails here even if it lints clean, and so does one with a solid area its form doesn't allow. Under the header, the only solid area is the zones' baseline; everything else is a hairline mark or the bracket. In place of the header, the only solid areas are the header's own bar and the window of keys, or for a sample, the sample's own silhouette and its two markers over the black backing.
- **It doesn't answer notes.** The display input has note activity but no pitch (`draw.hpp`, `Input`), so a keyboard map can't show the key under the player's finger, and it doesn't flare either: a note is answered by the drawing (`craft.md`, Motion). The map is still.
- **Context, not a control's channel.** The bracket sliding along the ruler clears the 24 px position floor but changes too little of the screen to pass a control's perceptibility alone; the control still has to move the drawing.
- **No leader lines.** A straight line from the moving bracket to a fixed corner would have to turn and change length as the bracket moves. A node can turn about the corner in the screen's plane, but its scale is uniform only (`constraints.md`, Node scale), so lengthening it would thicken it too. The only other way is to reshape it on every edit, which spends a mutable outline. The matching marks do the job for free.
- **Don't repeat the header.** The header shows the value in real units; the map shows where it sits.
- **One strip at rest.** Header, map, drawing and P5's bottom strip make four bands, which is a panel. With a context map, a bottom strip only shows while its own control is in use. A map in the header is the strip: never a second one under it.
- **No values means the drawing carries everything.** With the header replaced, nothing on screen says "62". Every control still has to read in the drawing at 0, 50 and 100 (`perceptibility.py`), and a control the drawing can't show is a reason to keep the header.
- **Leaving draft.** The server never draws a discipline into a design pass, so I try it on purpose, as the focus of a frames pass. It stops being a draft when an audited library screen uses it and its card says what the map added.

changes.find: The exception is a page where the interaction is the picture: choosing notes on a keyboard, shaping a filter curve.

One more: a context strip (P16) stays at rest when the controls select part of a whole the drawing doesn't show, and I can say in one sentence what it tells the player that the drawing doesn't. Under the header it's drawn as a static locator in the drawing's own language, never as a filled bar, a slider or a row of cells; in place of the header it takes the header's own bar. It can stand over another kind of whole if the screen says why, but never without that one sentence: a map of nothing the player needs is a panel.

Reviewed revision 11 in parallel with the audit: changes_requested, 4 findings (close-up from overview bins; markers follow what bounds the close-up; settle or drop the under-header sample form; overlap the halves instead of a gap). Not recorded as a verdict since the audit sent it back; folded into revision 12.
findings: 1. Say what a sampler's close-up is drawn from. The screen gets only the 96-bin overview of the whole sample (constraints.md, Sample engine), so it can't show the sample at waveform resolution between the markers. mock-sample.png draws a made-up multi-cycle sine for a region of about 15 bins, which teaches the next designer a zoom the device can't produce. State that the close-up is built from the overview bins in the selected region, or is a figure driven by the engine's own controls, and redraw the mock that way.

2. The markers must mark the part the close-up shows; that's the map's whole job. 'A sample as the map' ties them to the overview's begin and end, but 'A sampler' lists the loop, a slice and a grain window as close-ups. The stock loop points aren't in the display input, and slices and grain windows are the engine's own controls. Say the markers follow whatever bounds the close-up, either the outer markers (stock or stockShift) or the engine's own controls through Input, and drop 'the loop' unless the engine has its own loop controls.

3. Settle the under-header sample form. 'Under the header the same build fits the slimmer strip' contradicts the pitfall 'Under the header, the only solid area is the zones' baseline', and nothing says whether the under-header form uses the bracket or the squares, or how it ties to the frame's corner marks. Either specify it (height, marker form, the tie to the frame) and update the pitfall, or limit the sample form to in place of the header for now.

4. Overlap the two silhouette halves by 1 px instead of leaving a 2 px gap. In P16 a gap in the baseline means a split, and at 1:1 the notch at x 240 makes the sample look cut in two. Same-grey fills can overlap safely, as the mock's own ribbons do so they don't just touch.

Reviewed revision 12 in parallel with the audit: changes_requested, 3 findings (close-up as joined vertices like the band, not flat steps; keep the one-sentence test hard, only which wholes qualify is a default; exact close-up overlap). Folded into revision 13.
findings: 1. Replace the flat-step close-up with the band's own drawing: the same 32 points as vertices (each a bin's high or low, joined by straight lines, still from the bins between the markers, still no finer than the overview). At 1:1 the 24 px steps read as a column chart, not the OP-XY. They break One drawing language, because the band draws the same sample as joined points. They also show only half the data the point budget allows (8 bins a half instead of 16). Keep the sentence about not inventing detail; joining real bin values with straight lines doesn't. Re-render mock-sample.png and check it at 1:1.

2. In 'When it's there' and the matching craft.md sentence, make only the first condition (which wholes qualify) a breakable default. The one-sentence test of what the map tells the player that the drawing doesn't should hold every time, because the pattern itself says 'a map of nothing the player needs is a panel'. Suggested wording: 'A screen can use it for a whole outside these, saying why in a sentence, but never without the one sentence of what the map tells the player.'
3. In 'The sample's close-up', replace 'overlapping a few pixels' with an exact value, as the band does (2 px), so the two halves are built the same way in both places.

Reviewed revision 13 in parallel with the audit: changes_requested, 2 findings (close-up plateaus for short stretches, interpolate instead; craft.md header wording vs P8 own header). Folded into revision 14.
findings: 1. The close-up still steps for short stretches. 'When the stretch is shorter than 32 bins, bins repeat across groups' gives pairs of points at the same height, so the outline becomes flat plateaus, and mock-sample.svg shows exactly that (e.g. 163.8 and 176.67 both at y 89.82). Most close-ups are shorter than 32 bins, so this is the common case. Replace repetition with linear interpolation: put the 32 points at even x across the stretch and give each the value on the straight line between the two nearest bin centres (highest high on top, lowest low below). The outline is then a polyline through the real bin values with extra collinear points that don't show, which still invents nothing and matches the band. Keep max/min grouping for stretches of 32 bins or more. Update the 'The sample's close-up' bullet and regenerate mock-sample.png/.svg from mock_sample.py so the close-up has no plateaus at 1:1.

2. Small wording fix in craft.md: 'The one time the header goes is a P16 context map in its place' reads as if it excludes P8's existing 'Own header' option, which also covers y 0-20. Reword so the two agree, e.g. 'The one time the header gives up its titles and values is a P16 context map in its place, for a machine with at most four controls; an own header (P8) rebuilds it rather than removing it.'
